topics: Instant messaging app — encryption, character encoding, file compression, ergonomics, centralised storage and privacy

stem.text: WAPP company develops an instant messaging application. Mary uses the application in her tablet computer to communicate with her friends.
The application provides an encryption function so that all messages can be encrypted before sending. Give a benefit and a drawback of this function.
Benefit: ______

points.point: Benefit: Messages are protected from eavesdropping and interception. (better data security)
Drawback: Take time to do the encryption.

markingScheme.modelAnswer: Benefit: messages are protected from eavesdropping and interception (better data security). Drawback: time is taken to do the encryption.

stem.text: The application allows users to send messages with symbols such as ☺ and ☎. However, the symbols are not represented as images in computer storage. Explain how the symbols are represented and the benefit of representing them in this way.

so that the size of the messages (storage required) can be reduced.

markingScheme.modelAnswer: The symbols are stored and sent as character codes (text), not images, which reduces the size of the messages (storage required).

stem.text: Mary uses the tablet computer to take a video and send it to her friend, Billy, through the application. She finds that the video Billy receives has a smaller file size than the original. Give two benefits of reducing the file size of the video.

points.point: Reduce time for file transmission. (network traffic)
Reduce data storage needed for the recipient's device. (storage space)

markingScheme.modelAnswer: Shorter file transmission time (less network traffic) and less data storage needed on the recipient's device.

stem.text: Mary regularly uses the application with the tablet computer for four hours continuously every day in her workplace. Give a health problem that she may encounter and suggest a way to minimise the problem.

Way to minimise: She should take a 5-minute break after using the tablet computer for every 30 minutes. / ergonomic-designed furniture

markingScheme.modelAnswer: Health problem: neck pain/fatigue (alternatives: eyes, arms). Minimise it by taking a 5-minute break after every 30 minutes of use, or by using ergonomic-designed furniture.

stem.text: WAPP company requests Mary to store her data, such as contact list, previous messages and multimedia files, in its centralised servers through the application.
(i) Give two possible uses of the users' data stored in the centralised servers that can benefit Mary.

points.point: One valid use (any one of): It helps the recovery of users' contact lists/previous messages through the Internet. / The data in the tablet computer can be deleted so as to save its storage space. / Maintain the consistency of data for multiple devices.
A second, different valid use from the same list.

markingScheme.modelAnswer: Any two of: recovery of contact lists/previous messages through the Internet; the data on the tablet can be deleted to save its storage space; consistency of data across multiple devices.

stem.text: Suggest two possible privacy threats posed by this request.

points.point: One valid threat (any one of): WAPP company may distribute/misuse the contact lists of users for other commercial activities. / WAPP company may reveal users' privacy in their private conversations. / The server will attract more hacking as it has much more privacy information.

stem.text: Suggest two different network controls that can ensure that each student can only connect one mobile device to the school network.

stem.text: Assume that there is no overhead during network transmission. Estimate the minimum time taken for each of the following activities.
(i) Upload 500 MB image files from a customer's mobile device to a server through the Internet.

points.point: The bottleneck is the broadband upload speed (50 Mbps), so time = 500 x 8 / 50

markingScheme.modelAnswer: 500 x 8 / 50 = 80 s (limited by the 50 Mbps upload speed of the broadband connection).

points.point: The bottleneck is the wired connection (100 Mbps), so time = 1024 x 8 / 100

markingScheme.modelAnswer: 1024 x 8 / 100 = 82 s (or 80 s). The staff computer's wired connection (100 Mbps), not the 300 Mbps broadband download speed, is the bottleneck.

stem.text: A customer tries to use his mobile device to download some image files through the wireless connection, but the download speed is much slower than 54 Mbps. Give three possible reasons.

points.point: One valid reason (any one of): There is a network interruption/interference in the coffee shop. / A maximum bandwidth is set. / More than one device are connected to the network. / Overheads. / Poor reception of the network signal due to an unstable connection. / Network devices in a location with poor reception / obstacles.
A second, different valid reason from the same list (1x3 in total).
A third, different valid reason from the same list.

stem.text: The IP address of the IP camera is 192.168.0.8. John, a staff member of the coffee shop, wants to connect to the IP camera through the staff computer and the home computer.
(i) Which computer(s) can John use to connect to the IP camera through the following IP addresses?
(2) The fixed IP address of the broadband connection  ______

points.point: (1) Staff computer (only, because 192.168.0.8 is a private address reachable inside the shop's LAN)
(2) Staff computer and home computer (the fixed public IP address is reachable through the Internet)

stem.text: John is worried about eavesdropping on the IP camera although password protection is in place. Give a security measure that can minimise this threat.

points.point: VPN channel / Encryption

markingScheme.modelAnswer: Use a VPN channel / encryption so the camera traffic cannot be read even if intercepted.

stem.text: The coffee shop expands the existing computer network with a proxy server. There are two designs, as follows:
Design A: Internet — Router — Proxy server (the proxy server is placed behind the router, inside the network).
Design B: Internet — Proxy server — Router (the proxy server is placed in front of the router, facing the Internet).
(i) In general, which design is more commonly used? Justify your answer.

points.point: A justified choice, e.g. Design A: the router can first scan through the incoming message so as to reduce the loading of the proxy server. (The scheme alternatively accepts Design B: the proxy server can hide the IP addresses of the devices.)

The justification is completed consistently: ...so as to provide higher security level for the network (Design B) / the loading argument is carried through for Design A. (2 marks in total for the choice with matching justification.)

markingScheme.modelAnswer: Design A — the router first scans incoming messages, reducing the proxy server's loading. (The booklet also accepts Design B, justified by the proxy hiding the devices' IP addresses to give a higher security level.)

stem.text: Explain how a proxy server can improve customers' Internet browsing experience.

points.point: It temporarily stores some web pages once a network user has visited (recently visited) them.

When other network users visit the web pages, they can directly access those stored in the proxy server rather than downloading the web pages through the Internet again, leading to saving time on download. (speed of access) (2* in total)

markingScheme.modelAnswer: The proxy caches recently visited web pages; later visitors get them from the proxy instead of downloading them from the Internet again, which speeds up access.

stem.text: Give another function of a proxy server, other than the function in (d)(ii).

markingScheme.modelAnswer: Filtering indecent web sites, or recording browsing history.

topics: Private network design — duplex mode, synchronous transmission, circuit vs packet switching, packet headers, packet-count and transfer-time calculation

stem.text: Peter develops a private network for users to send text messages and files through, and to dial phone calls.
Peter considers using the following designs for the private network. Briefly describe each design and its characteristics.
(i) Duplex communication mode

points.point: Shows an understanding of the duplex communication mode (both stations can transmit and receive).
Advantage: simultaneous communication.

markingScheme.modelAnswer: In duplex mode, data can be transmitted in both directions simultaneously, so both parties can send and receive at the same time.

stem.text: Synchronous transmission

points.point: Shows an understanding of synchronous transmission (data is sent in a synchronised stream/blocks timed by a clock signal, without start/stop bits for each character).
Advantage: lower overhead / higher throughput.

markingScheme.modelAnswer: In synchronous transmission, data is sent in blocks in step with a clock signal, without per-character start/stop bits; the lower overhead gives a higher throughput.

stem.text: Circuit switching

points.point: Shows an understanding of circuit switching (a circuit is set up between the two parties before communication and held for its duration).
Advantage: a dedicated connection.

markingScheme.modelAnswer: In circuit switching, a dedicated connection (circuit) is established between sender and receiver before data is sent and is reserved until the communication ends.

stem.text: Peter decides to use packet switching in the network. When sending a file, a number of packets will be sent and each packet consists of a header and a payload which is the actual data to be sent.
(i) Give three pieces of information that are stored in the header.

points.point: One valid item (any one of): source address / destination address / length of the packet / checksum / identification tag / priority (Quality of Service) / hop count / TTL (Time to live) / port number.
A second, different valid item from the same list (1x3 in total).
A third, different valid item from the same list.

markingScheme.modelAnswer: Any three of: source address, destination address, packet length, checksum, identification tag, priority (QoS), hop count/TTL, port number.

stem.text: Packets are sent to a receiver through different routes. What will be done at the receiver to process the packets?

points.point: A checksum will be calculated for error checking.
The data packets are reassembled in the correct order.

markingScheme.modelAnswer: The receiver checks each packet (checksum) for errors and reassembles the packets in the correct order to recover the file.

points.point: = 2132 packets (rounded up, as a part packet still needs one packet)

points.point: Choose 600 dpi. (For reference: at 600 dpi the paper needs 8x600 = 4800 by 10x600 = 6000 dots; at 2400 dpi it would need 8x2400 = 19200 by 10x2400 = 24000 dots — the scheme notes that no calculation is required.)
Justification: 600 dpi should be chosen for the photos with the resolution 5472x3648. Otherwise, the printouts of the photos on the 8R photo paper would be very small for using 2400dpi.

stem.text: Customers can use their photos to generate animation in GIF or SWF format. Give three major differences of the two formats.

stem.text: The studio finds that a browser displays its web page on two computers differently, as shown below:

stem.text: Suggest a web page design solution to solve the problem in (d)(i).

stem.text: A customer takes photos with the same camera and settings and save the photos with the same compression method. He finds that the file sizes of the photos are different from each other. Why? Explain briefly.

With the same compression method, the compositions of the compressed data of the photos are different (e.g. the number of colours). / After compression, the file sizes of the photos with simple shapes and colour combination are smaller.

markingScheme.modelAnswer: Lossy/lossless compression acts on the photo content: photos with simpler shapes and fewer colours compress to smaller files, so identical settings still give different file sizes.

stem.text: A customer considers using JPG, RAW and TIFF formats for photo-taking.

stem.text: Give an advantage of using TIFF over RAW.

unacceptable: Bare claims 'contain metadata / no compression' are marked ✗.
markingScheme.modelAnswer: E.g. TIFF can be viewed/edited by common software without a dedicated RAW converter, and it can maintain layers.

topics: HK Cinema mobile web site — GPS services, client-side vs server-side scripts, login methods and security, mobile layout design

stem.text: HK Cinema owns several cinemas in different districts. Customers can use an online ticketing service on its web site to buy movie tickets. Mr Li is the IT manager of the company. He is going to develop a mobile version of the web site for customers to browse on a smartphone.

points.point: One valid example (services using both user locations and cinema locations): Find the closest cinemas.
A second valid example: Suggest routes to cinemas (time/distance/navigation). / Navigation purposes. (1x2 in total)

unacceptable: Suitable language settings, street view, finding user/cinema location only, and checking cinemas for available seats are marked ✗ (they do not use both locations / are not GPS-based services).
markingScheme.modelAnswer: E.g. find the closest cinemas to the customer, and suggest routes to a cinema with time/distance/navigation.

stem.text: When each of the following tasks is carried out in the web site, should a client-side script or a server-side script be used? Justify your answer.
(i) Check the availability of seats for a certain show time.

points.point: Server-side script (concept of server-side).
Explanation: The data of the available seats is stored in the database in the server.

unacceptable: An explanation about buying tickets, such as updating the seats in the database, is marked ✗.
markingScheme.modelAnswer: A server-side script, because seat availability data is stored in the database on the server.

stem.text: Check whether the number of movie tickets to be bought is greater than 0.

points.point: Client-side script (concept of client-side).
Explanation: The checking/response time on the client-side is shorter. / Reduce the server loading.

unacceptable: Explanations such as 'checking the number of tickets is correct', 'server-side scripts are not needed', 'checking can be done by a browser only' or 'higher efficiency' are marked ✗.
markingScheme.modelAnswer: A client-side script: the simple input check is done immediately in the browser, shortening response time and reducing server loading.

(i) Suggest another example of biometric authentication for Mr Li to consider.

unacceptable: 'Pupil' or 'eye' alone is marked ✗.
markingScheme.modelAnswer: E.g. facial recognition (or iris/retinal scanning, hand geometry, palm veins, voice).

stem.text: Method 2: Draw a pattern with straight lines. [The figure shows a 3x3 grid of dots with a Z-shaped pattern drawn by connecting dots with straight lines.]
(ii) Suggest an improvement on the design to enhance the security.

points.point: Any one of: Use a board with 4x4 dots (more than 9 dots). / Set a minimum number of dots to be connected. / Hide the drawn lines.

unacceptable: 'Add passwords or other forms of authentication' and 'use more complicated patterns' are marked ✗.
markingScheme.modelAnswer: E.g. hide the drawn lines (or use a 4x4 dot board, or require a minimum number of connected dots).

stem.text: Method 3: Input a sequence of digits on a keypad where buttons of the 10 digits are randomly displayed on different positions for each login. [The figure shows the keypad buttons in a scrambled order: 3, 8, 5 / 4, 9, 7 / 0, 2, 6 and 1.]
(iii) Give a reason to support the random display.

points.point: Any one of: Hackers cannot get the password by acquiring mouse click locations. / (nor) by hand movement / Make sure that user is human / it is not a robot program.

unacceptable: 'Stop key logger', 'hacker cannot keep trying login', 'it is difficult to get the password' and 'increase security' are marked ✗ as bare claims.
markingScheme.modelAnswer: Because the digit positions change each time, an observer (or malware) cannot recover the password from the click positions/hand movements; it also shows the user is human, not a robot program.

topics: Text editor UNDO/REDO — stack operations, full-stack handling, testing stages, programming-language selection

stem.text: John is going to develop a text editor. Only words will be typed into the editor. He uses two stacks S1 and S2 to set up an UNDO button and a REDO button. S1 stores the current typed words while S2 is temporary storage. When the UNDO button is clicked, the latest typed word will be removed from S1. When the REDO button is clicked, the latest removed word will be restored to S1.
For example, after the sentence 'MATHEMATICAL REASONING MAY BE REGARDED' is typed, the contents of S1 and S2 are:

stem.caption: S1 after typing (position 1 is the bottom)

stem.text: When the UNDO button is clicked twice, the contents of S1 and S2 are:
Describe the stack operations involving S1 and S2 for the following cases.
(i) The UNDO button is clicked.

points.point: POP S1, then PUSH (the popped word onto) S2.

markingScheme.modelAnswer: Pop the top word from S1 and push it onto S2.

stem.text: The REDO button is clicked.

points.point: POP S2, then PUSH (the popped word onto) S1.

markingScheme.modelAnswer: Pop the top word from S2 and push it back onto S1.

stem.text: S1 is empty and the UNDO button is clicked.

points.point: No action

markingScheme.modelAnswer: Nothing happens — no stack operation is performed.

stem.text: Assume that S2 is full. Suggest a way to handle these stacks.

points.point: A notification will be issued. (Scheme alternative: remove the bottommost element of S2, then POP S1 and PUSH S2.)

markingScheme.modelAnswer: Issue a notification that no more UNDO is possible (or make room by removing the bottommost element of S2 before pushing).

stem.text: When developing the text editor, acceptance testing, system testing and unit testing will be carried out. Give the correct sequence of the testing stages and explain briefly the use of each testing stage.

points.point: Correct sequence: unit testing → system testing → acceptance testing.
Use of unit testing: test each subprogram/module separately.
Use of system testing: test the whole integrated system as one system.
Use of acceptance testing: check with the users that the system meets their requirements before it is accepted.

markingScheme.modelAnswer: Unit testing (individual subprograms) first, then system testing (the whole system), then acceptance testing (users verify the system meets their needs).

points.point: Z

markingScheme.modelAnswer: Z: X (10110001) and Y (10110010) each contain four 1s (even), while Z (10110101) contains five 1s (odd), so Z fails the even parity check.

stem.text: Occasionally some errors cannot be detected. Why not? Explain your answer with an example.

points.point: If an even number of bits are in error, the number of 1s keeps the same parity, so the parity check still passes and the error is not detected

points.point: Check the channel to ensure being clear before sending a packet.
Otherwise wait for a random period of time (backoff factor/backoff counter). The steps are repeated until all packets are sent.

stem.text: Tom writes a subprogram F1 to process a global integer array, A, of size n. The pseudocode for F1 is:

stem.code:
Subprogram F1
    isStop <- FALSE
    pos <- n - 1
    while isStop <> TRUE do
        if A[pos] = 1 then
            A[pos] <- 0
            pos <- pos - 1
        else
            A[pos] <- 1
            isStop <- TRUE

stem.text: Suppose that n = 8.

m to the value in A (it adds the input parameter m, not a fixed amount)

stem.text: Based on the draft of the ER diagram, create a database schema in Third Normal Form without derived attributes. Identify the corresponding primary keys and foreign keys. Write 'N/A' if not applicable.

stem.text: Below are sample records of RENTAL:
If a storage box has never been rented, there is no record of the storage box in RENTAL.

points.point: SELECT LOC, COUNT(SBOX.SID) AS AVAILABLE FROM SBOX (the alias AS AVAILABLE is blacked out in the scan but legible underneath)
WHERE OUTOFSER = FALSE AND (the scheme adds the alternative '(or NOT OUTOFSERV)', as printed)

FROM SBOX
WHERE OUTOFSER = FALSE AND

GROUP BY LOC
HAVING COUNT(SBOX.SID) < 10

points.point: Counts the drivers for each bus route (the DRIVENO view: SELECT BROUTE.BID, COUNT(*) AS TOTAL FROM BROUTE, DRIVER WHERE BROUTE.BID = DRIVER.BID GROUP BY BROUTE.BID)
Groups the count by route (GROUP BY BROUTE.BID)
Compares the count with the number of buses and lists the routes: SELECT BROUTE.BID FROM BROUTE, DRIVENO WHERE BROUTE.BID = DRIVENO.BID AND TOTAL < BNO

markingScheme.modelAnswer:
CREATE VIEW DRIVENO AS
SELECT BROUTE.BID, COUNT(*) AS TOTAL FROM BROUTE, DRIVER
WHERE BROUTE.BID = DRIVER.BID
GROUP BY BROUTE.BID

SELECT BROUTE.BID FROM BROUTE, DRIVENO
WHERE BROUTE.BID = DRIVENO.BID AND TOTAL < BNO

SELECT BROUTE.BID
FROM BROUTE, DRIVER
WHERE BROUTE.BID=DRIVER.BID
GROUP BY BROUTE.BID
HAVING COUNT(BROUTE.BID) < AVG(BNO)   (MAX or MIN)

SELECT BID FROM BROUTE
WHERE BNO >
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM DRIVER
   WHERE BROUTE.BID=DRIVER.BID

stem.text: In a train station, the departure times of trains in one day are stored in an array P of size n ordered by time. Peter writes a program F1(s, t) to find the number of trains departed from time s to time t inclusive. He assumes that there are always trains departed at time s and time t. For example, according to the content of P below, F1(12:20, 18:00) returns 3.
Peter writes a subprogram BS using binary search to find the index of the train departed at time t:

stem.code:
BS(t)
  s <- 1
  e <- n
  while s <= e do
    m <- (s+e)/2
    if P[m] = t then
      exit subprogram and return m
    else
      if t > P[m] then
        s <- m + 1
      else
        e <- m - 1
  return m

stem.text: According to the content of P above, find the return values of the following: (1) F1(07:10, 14:25); (2) F1(11:25, 11:25).
Complete the following pseudocode for F1.

stem.code:
F1(s, t)
  count <- 0
  for i from 1 to n do
    if _____ AND _____ then
      count <- _____
  return count

points.point: First blank: s <= P[i]
Second blank: P[i] <= t (the scheme notes that giving both comparisons without the '=' signs, i.e. s < P[i] and P[i] < t, earns only 1 mark for the pair)
count <- count + 1

markingScheme.modelAnswer: if (s <= P[i]) AND (P[i] <= t) then count <- count + 1.

stem.text: Refer to the content of P above. What is the return value of BS(14:25)?

points.point: 5 (trace: s=1, e=7, m=4 gives P[4]=12:20 < 14:25 so s=5; m=6 gives P[6]=18:00 > 14:25 so e=5; m=5 gives P[5]=14:25, found, return 5)

Peter rewrites F1 as F2. F2 uses binary search to find the index of the train departed at time s. Then it sequentially searches the number of trains departed on or before time t. Complete the pseudocode for F2 below.

F2(s, t)
  count <- 0
  for i from BS( _____ ) to n do

      count <- count + 1
  return count

points.point: Blank in the for statement: s (the scan starts at BS(s), the index of the first train in range)
Condition blank: P[i] <= t (equivalently i <= BS(t)); the scheme notes that the strict versions P[i] < t or i < BS(t) earn only 1 of these 2 marks

markingScheme.modelAnswer: for i from BS(s) to n do; if P[i] <= t then count <- count + 1.
